newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers in Oklahoma City bomb case end arguments.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers in Oklahoma City bomb case end arguments.

text.p: The evidence against each of the defendants in the Oklahoma City bombing case contrasts so sharply it would be unfair to try the two men together, a defence lawyer argued in a pre-trial hearing Thursday.

Defendants Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols, charged in the April 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that claimed the lives of 168 people, were seeking to have their trials separated.
On Wednesday experts testified on the severance motion and on Thursday lawyers concluded their arguments.
Sean Connelly said the two defendants should be tried together because 95 percent of the evidence applied to both defendants.
U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch was expected to rule on the defence motion for severance in several weeks.
The date for the actual trial was not set but was expected to begin in the first half of 1997.
Nichols' attorney Michael Tigar said his defendant was at home in Kansas on the day of the bombing and nowhere near the bomb site.

"On the morning of April 19, 1995, somebody got out of a (rental) truck and ignited a fuse. Whoever that was could see the people in that building and see them going in and out," Tigar told the court. He said that person would be in a very different situation than his defendant.

McVeigh's attorneys were concerned about statements Nichols made two days after the bombing when he spoke for 9-1/2 hours with local police in Herington, Kansas, and mentioned McVeigh's name at least 60 times.
The statements could only be used as evidence against Nichols, but defence attorneys argued it would be too much to ask of jurors to ignore the references to McVeigh.
Tiger told reporters later that his burden was "to prove that Timothy McVeigh is a liar and (McVeigh's attorney) Mr. (Stephen) Jones is going to have to try to show that Terry Nichols is a liar."
Matsch showed his concern about the issue when he said that if the Nichols statement were also used to prove any falsehoods and incriminate Nichols it could also incriminate a co-defendant.
In other issues Matsch kept under seal court filings that the press had wanted opened.
Matsch also quashed subpoenas for information from government agencies that McVeigh's attorneys sought.
Prosecutors are obliged to give defendants information it comes across that might help them. The prosecution said it complied with its duty.
But Jones was not convinced. "I believe there's a coverup going on here. I believe information is being withheld from us and possibly from the prosecution," he told the court.
As an example Jones said the prosecution provided the court under seal information about an unspecified "specific incident" that occurred the day of the bombing.
"That information is absolutely criticial to Mr McVeigh's defence," Jones said in court without elaborating.
Jones said the government provided small amounts of information, but not enough.
